title: Distributions on trial
goal: Weigh the trials and meta-analyses comparing polarised, pyramidal and threshold training, read their effect sizes, and state both sides of the polarised debate and why athlete level may matter.

steps.title: The first trials: polarised vs threshold
steps.text:
Trials began by pitting polarised training against threshold-heavy training. In an [RCT](g:rct) of 48 well-trained runners, cyclists, triathletes and skiers over 9 weeks, the polarised group raised [VO2peak](g:vo2peak) most: **+11.7%** [[c:ie-stoggl]]. In a [crossover study](g:crossover-study) of 12 trained male cyclists, 6 weeks polarised beat 6 weeks threshold for peak power (**8% vs 3%**) and lactate threshold power (**9% vs 2%**), even with about an hour less training per week [[c:ie-neal]].

Note the comparison: these trials tested polarised against **threshold** plans: lots of zone 2 and little or no zone 3 (Neal's was 57/43/0 by time). Elite athletes mostly train **pyramidal**. Beating threshold training says little about beating pyramidal.

claims.text: In 48 well-trained endurance athletes over 9 weeks, polarised training gave the largest VO2peak gain (+11.7%), more than threshold, HIIT or high-volume training.

evidence.quote: POL demonstrated the greatest increase in VO2peak (+6.8 ml·min·kg(-1) or 11.7%, P < 0.001), time to exhaustion during the ramp protocol (+17.4%, P < 0.001) and peak velocity/power (+5.1%, P < 0.01).

claims.text: In 12 trained male cyclists, 6 weeks of polarised training improved peak power (8% vs 3%) and lactate threshold (9% vs 2%) more than threshold training, on fewer hours (6.4 vs 7.5 h per week).

evidence.quote: Improvements were greater following polarized rather than threshold for PPO [mean (±SE) change of 8 (±2)% vs. 3 (±1)%, P < 0.05], LT [9 (±3)% vs. 2 (±4)%, P < 0.05], and high-intensity exercise capacity [85 (±14)% vs. 37 (±14)%, P < 0.05].

1) a polarized model [6.4 (±1.4 SD) h/wk; 80%, 0%, and 20% of training time in low-, moderate-, and high-intensity zones, respectively]; and 2) a threshold model [7.5 (±2.0 SD) h/wk; 57%, 43%, and 0% training-intensity distribution]

steps.title: The first meta-analysis (2019)
steps.text:
Rosenblat and colleagues pooled the [RCTs](g:rct) comparing polarised with threshold training in athletes with over 2 years of training. Only **4 studies** qualified, **3** could be pooled. Their quality was fair to poor: 4 or 5 out of 10 on the [PEDro scale](g:pedro-scale) [[c:ie-ros19-quality]].

On time-trial performance the pooled [effect size](g:effect-size) was **−0.66** (95% [CI](g:confidence-interval) −1.17 to −0.15) [[c:ie-ros19-effect]]. Negative here means a bigger drop in time-trial time, so it favours polarised training, a moderate effect.

A moderate effect, but from three small, fair-quality trials against threshold training only: promising, not settled.

claims.text: Only four RCTs met the criteria (three meta-analysed), scoring 4–5 out of 10 on the PEDro scale.

evidence.quote: Four studies met the inclusion criteria for the qualitative analysis, and 3 for the meta-analysis. Two of the 4 studies included in the review scored a 4/10 on the PEDro Scale and 2 scored a 5/10.

claims.text: Pooled, polarised training improved time-trial performance more than threshold training (ES −0.66, 95% CI −1.17 to −0.15).

evidence.quote: The pooled results demonstrate a moderate effect (ES = -0.66; 95% CI: -1.17 to -0.15) favoring the POL group over the THR group.

steps.title: More trials, smaller effects (2024)
steps.text:
By 2024 there were **17 studies, 437 participants**, now comparing polarised with any other distribution, pyramidal included. Most participants were men (317 men, 89 women) [[c:ie-oli-sample]].

Results, as a [standardised mean difference](g:standardised-mean-difference) (SMD; 0.2 small, 0.5 medium):

- **VO2peak**: polarised slightly better, SMD **0.24** [[c:ie-oli-vo2]]. But only in interventions shorter than 12 weeks and in highly trained athletes [[c:ie-oli-subgroups]].
- **Time trial, time to exhaustion, threshold speed or power**: no difference [[c:ie-oli-null]].

So: a small edge on one lab marker, none on performance itself.

claims.text: Seventeen studies (437 participants, 317 men and 89 women) compared polarised with other distributions.

evidence.quote: The total number of participants included was n = 437 (317 males, 89 females, 31 undisclosed), of which 183 participated in POL interventions and 223 in other TIDs.

claims.text: Polarised training improved VO2peak slightly more than other distributions (SMD 0.24).

evidence.quote: POL is superior to other TIDs for improving VO2peak, particularly in shorter duration interventions and highly trained athletes.

claims.text: The VO2peak advantage appeared only in interventions under 12 weeks and in highly trained athletes.

evidence.quote: Superiority, however, only occurred in shorter interventions (< 12 weeks)
and for highly trained athletes (SMD = 0.46 [95% CI 0.10, 0.82]

claims.text: Time trial, time to exhaustion and speed or power at the second threshold improved similarly with polarised and other distributions.

evidence.quote: The remaining endurance performance surrogates were similarly affected by POL and other TIDs

steps.title: Polarised vs pyramidal, and the athlete's level
steps.text:
A 2025 [network meta-analysis](g:network-meta-analysis) re-analysed each participant's own data from 13 studies (348 athletes). Polarised and pyramidal did not differ for VO2max or time trial, and no distribution beat polarised [[c:ie-ros25-null]]. A [subgroup analysis](g:subgroup-analysis) hinted that competitive athletes gain more VO2max from polarised and recreational athletes from pyramidal [[c:ie-ros25-level]]. A 2026 Bayesian network meta-analysis also found no model clearly better than polarised, though its rankings leaned towards threshold training for VO2max and HIIT for time trial [[c:ie-li]].

Timing may matter more than shape: in 60 well-trained male runners, 8 weeks pyramidal then 8 weeks polarised gave the biggest 5 km gain (about 1.5%) [[c:ie-filipas]].

Subgroup results are hints, not proof: treat 'level matters' as an idea to test, not a finding.

claims.text: In an individual-participant network meta-analysis (13 studies, 348 athletes), no distribution differed significantly from polarised for VO2max or time trial.

evidence.quote: There were no statistically significant differences between POL and any of the other TID interventions.

claims.text: Competitive athletes may gain more VO2max from polarised and recreational athletes from pyramidal training.

evidence.quote: Athletes at a more competitive level may benefit from a POL TID intervention and recreational athletes from a PYR TID intervention.

claims.text: A 2026 Bayesian network meta-analysis found no distribution with a definite advantage over polarised for VO2max or time trial, though its rankings favoured threshold training for VO2max and HIIT for time trial.

evidence.quote: Compared with polarized training, no other TID model showed a definite advantage for improving V̇ o2 max or TT performance, because all 95% credible intervals crossed zero.
However, Bayesian posterior ranking indicated that lactate-threshold training (THR) was most likely to be the optimal model for
whereas high-intensity interval training (HIT) was most likely to optimize TT performance

claims.text: In 60 well-trained runners over 16 weeks, switching from pyramidal to polarised gave the largest improvements, including about 1.5% in 5 km time.

evidence.quote: However, the change from pyramidal to polarized distribution maximized performance improvements

steps.title: The debate, both sides
steps.text:
In 2022 two groups argued it out in the same journal. Foster, Seiler and colleagues: observational and trial data show polarised (or pyramidal) training beats threshold-centred training, and it may matter most for elites, who train a lot and risk maladaptation [[c:ie-foster]]. Burnley, Bearden and Jones: elites mostly train pyramidal, polarised has not been shown to beat other distributions, and zone 2 work is effective and specific to races lasting about 25 min to 3 h [[c:ie-burnley]].

Read closely, they agree on a lot: mostly zone 1, some hard work, and zone 2 should not be the largest share. The real dispute is how to share the hard part between zones 2 and 3.

claims.text: Foster and colleagues argue a polarised (including pyramidal) distribution has advantages over threshold-centred training, particularly for elite athletes with high training loads.

evidence.quote: Abundant observational and interventional data support the concept that this TID has advantages over threshold centric training programs
The polarized/pyradimal TID may be particularly important for elite athletes, with high training frequency/load and a greater risk of training maladaptations

claims.text: Burnley and colleagues argue polarised distributions are neither more effective than others nor common among endurance athletes, who mostly train pyramidally.

evidence.quote: Polarized distributions of training volume have neither been shown to be more effective than other distributions, nor are they practiced commonly by endurance athletes; indeed pyramidal distributions are what highly successful athletes typically practice.

debate.question: Is polarised training the best intensity distribution for endurance athletes?

sides.position: Yes, broadly: polarised (or pyramidal) beats threshold-centred training, especially for elite athletes with heavy loads.
No: elites mostly train pyramidal, polarised hasn't been shown to beat pyramidal, and zone 2 work is effective and race-specific.

points: Early trials (Stöggl 2014, Neal 2013) found polarised beat threshold-heavy training, in small, short studies.
Rosenblat 2019: moderate effect for polarised over threshold on time trial, but only 3 pooled trials of fair quality.
Silva Oliveira 2024 (17 studies): small VO2peak edge for polarised (SMD 0.24), mainly in short studies and highly trained athletes; no difference in performance.
Rosenblat 2025 and Li 2026: no distribution clearly beats polarised; recreational athletes may do better with pyramidal (subgroup hint).
Both sides of the debate agree: mostly zone 1, some hard work, not zone 2 as the biggest share. The dispute is zone 2 vs zone 3 for the hard part.

variants.stem: A coach says: 'Trials show polarised beats threshold training, so my pyramidal runners should switch to polarised.' What is wrong with that step?

options.text: Those trials compared polarised with threshold, not with pyramidal
options.why: Right: beating a zone 2-heavy plan doesn't show polarised beats a pyramidal one.

options.text: The trials were in cyclists, not runners
options.why: Stöggl's trial included runners; the main gap is the comparator, not the sport.

options.text: Threshold and pyramidal are the same distribution
options.why: Threshold has zone 2 largest; pyramidal has zone 1 largest.

options.text: Polarised training has never been tested in an RCT
options.why: It has, for example the 48-athlete RCT by Stöggl and Sperlich.

variants.stem: Neal 2013 found polarised beat threshold training in 12 trained male cyclists over 6 weeks. Which limit matters most before applying it to a female age-group triathlete over a season?

options.text: Small sample, only men, and only 6 weeks
options.why: Right: 12 men over 6 weeks says little about women, other sports or a whole season.

options.text: The study used a crossover design
options.why: A crossover makes each rider his own control, which is a strength with small samples.

options.text: The polarised group trained more hours
options.why: The polarised group trained less: 6.4 vs 7.5 h per week.

options.text: Cycling performance can't be measured reliably
options.why: A 40 km time trial and power tests are standard, reliable measures.

variants.stem: A meta-analysis pools 3 small trials (PEDro 4–5/10) and finds a moderate effect for polarised over threshold on time trial. How strong is this evidence?

options.text: Weak: few, small trials of fair quality
options.why: Right: a pooled effect from three fair-quality trials is a promising signal, not a firm answer.

options.text: Strong: it is a meta-analysis of RCTs
options.why: Being a meta-analysis isn't enough; it is only as good as the few trials inside it.

options.text: Moderate: the confidence interval excludes zero
options.why: Excluding zero shows an effect is likely; it doesn't fix small, fair-quality trials.

options.text: Disputed: the effect is negative
options.why: The negative sign here favours polarised (time trial time fell more).

variants.stem: A meta-analysis reports polarised vs other distributions for VO2peak: SMD = 0.24 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.48). Best reading?

options.text: A small advantage for polarised, whose true size could be close to zero
options.why: Right: 0.24 is small, and the interval runs from almost nothing to under 0.5.

options.text: A large advantage: VO2peak rose 24% more
options.why: SMD is in units of spread, not percent; 0.24 is small.

options.text: No advantage, since 0.24 is below 0.5
options.why: An SMD of 0.24 is small but its interval excludes zero, so there is a small effect.

options.text: A medium advantage, because the upper limit is near 0.5
options.why: Judge the point estimate first; the upper limit is the most optimistic case.

variants.stem: The same meta-analysis reports time-trial performance: SMD = −0.01 (95% CI −0.28 to 0.25). Best reading?

options.text: No detectable difference between polarised and other distributions
options.why: Right: the estimate is almost zero and the interval runs both ways.

options.text: A small advantage for the other distributions
options.why: −0.01 is essentially zero; the interval includes clear benefit either way.

options.text: Polarised is worse by 1%
options.why: SMD is not a percentage; it is in units of spread.

options.text: A small advantage for polarised, because the upper limit is positive
options.why: An interval spanning zero can't show an advantage for either side.

variants.stem: A recreational cyclist on 6 h a week reads that 'polarised is superior for VO2peak (SMD 0.24)'. What should she take from it?

options.text: Little: a small edge, seen mainly in highly trained athletes
options.why: Right: the subgroup and outcome details make it weak guidance for her.

options.text: Switch to polarised: it is proven superior
options.why: It was superior only on VO2peak, by a small amount, mostly in highly trained athletes.

options.text: Avoid polarised: it doesn't improve performance
options.why: It improved performance as much as the other distributions, not less.

options.text: Ignore it: meta-analyses can't apply to individuals
options.why: Meta-analyses do apply, with care about who was studied.

variants.stem: Based on the 2025 individual-participant network meta-analysis, which athlete is the subgroup result most likely to favour pyramidal for?

options.text: A recreational marathon runner
options.why: Right: recreational athletes improved VO2max more with pyramidal in the subgroup analysis.

options.text: A national-level rower
options.why: Competitive athletes tended to gain more from polarised.

options.text: An elite cyclist in a heavy training block
options.why: Higher-level athletes leaned towards polarised.

options.text: Any athlete: the analysis showed pyramidal beats polarised overall
options.why: Overall there was no difference; only the subgroup hint split by level.

variants.stem: In Filipas 2022 (60 well-trained runners, 16 weeks), which plan gave the largest improvements?

options.text: 8 weeks pyramidal, then 8 weeks polarised
options.why: Right: the pyramidal-to-polarised switch gave the biggest gains, about 1.5% in 5 km time.

options.text: 16 weeks polarised
options.why: All groups improved, but the full polarised block was not the best.

options.text: 8 weeks polarised, then 8 weeks pyramidal
options.why: The reverse order did less well.

options.text: 16 weeks pyramidal
options.why: Pyramidal throughout improved, but less than switching to polarised.

variants.stem: Which summary of the 2022 polarised debate is fairest?

options.text: Both favour mostly zone 1 and some hard work; they differ on zone 2 vs zone 3
options.why: Right: they agree on the base and differ on how to share the hard part.

options.text: One side says train mostly easy, the other mostly at threshold
options.why: Burnley's side explicitly does not advocate threshold-centred training.

options.text: Both sides agree polarised is optimal for elites only
options.why: Burnley's side argues it isn't shown to be optimal for anyone.

options.text: The debate is settled by the 2024 meta-analysis
options.why: That meta-analysis found no performance difference; it didn't settle the debate.
